glossary.definition: Fasting; abstaining from food, drink, and other specified things from dawn until sunset. One of the Five Pillars of Islam. The Ramadan fast is obligatory for adult Muslims (with exemptions).
glossary.definitionAr: الإمساك عن المفطرات من الفجر إلى المغرب

glossary.definition: The pre-dawn meal eaten before Fajr. The last chance to eat and drink before the day's fast. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said there is blessing in suhoor.
The meal at sunset (Maghrib) when Muslims break the fast. Traditionally started with dates and water, then Maghrib prayer, then the main meal.
glossary.definitionAr: وجبة الإفطار عند المغرب؛ يبدأ بالتمر والماء

glossary.definition: The time to stop eating and drinking before Fajr. Fasting begins at Fajr; imsak is when one ceases intake (often a few minutes before Fajr in some regions).
glossary.definitionAr: وقت التوقف عن الأكل والشرب قبل الفجر

glossary.definition: Intention. The intention to fast must be made (in the heart) before dawn for the obligatory fast to be valid. Can be made once for the whole month or daily.
The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. The month of obligatory fasting, increased worship, and spiritual reflection. The Quran was first revealed in Ramadan.
The Night of Power (or Decree). One of the last ten odd nights of Ramadan. Worship on this night is better than that of a thousand months. The Quran was first revealed on this night.
glossary.definitionAr: خير من ألف شهر؛ ليلة نزول القرآن

glossary.definition: The new crescent moon. Sighting (or calculation) of the hilal marks the start of each Islamic month, including Ramadan and Shawwal (Eid al-Fitr).
Spiritual retreat in the mosque, devoting time to worship and remembrance. Often observed during the last ten nights of Ramadan, especially to seek Laylat al-Qadr.
The dawn prayer. First of the five daily prayers. Fasting begins at Fajr—no food or drink until Maghrib.
glossary.definitionAr: صلاة الفجر؛ يبدأ الصوم من بعدها

glossary.definition: The noon prayer, when the sun passes the meridian. One of the five daily prayers.
The afternoon prayer (mid-afternoon). One of the five daily prayers.
The sunset prayer. Time to break the fast (iftar). One of the five daily prayers.
The night prayer (after twilight). One of the five daily prayers. Taraweeh is performed after Isha during Ramadan.
Special voluntary prayers performed at night during Ramadan, after Isha. In many mosques, one thirtieth (juz) of the Quran is recited each night so the full Quran is completed by the end of Ramadan.
glossary.definitionAr: قيام الليل في رمضان بعد العشاء

glossary.definition: Prayer. The five daily obligatory prayers (Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha) are the second pillar of Islam.
The Festival of Breaking the Fast, celebrated on the first day of Shawwal after Ramadan. A day of joy, Eid prayer, charity (fitr), and community.
glossary.definitionAr: عيد بعد رمضان؛ يوم الفرح والصدقة

glossary.definition: The Festival of Sacrifice, celebrated on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah. Commemorates the obedience of Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Involves sacrifice and distribution of meat.
Obligatory charity; one of the Five Pillars. A portion of wealth (typically 2.5% of savings per year) given to those in need. Often calculated and given in Ramadan.
Voluntary charity given for the pleasure of Allah. Can be given at any time in any amount. Sadaqah Jariyah is ongoing charity (e.g. building a well, teaching).
Supplication; calling upon Allah. A personal conversation with God, made at any time. Especially encouraged when breaking the fast, in the last third of the night, and on Laylat al-Qadr.
Remembrance of Allah. Repeating phrases of praise and glorification (e.g. Subhan Allah, Alhamdulillah, Allahu Akbar) or other prescribed remembrances.
In the name of Allah. Said before eating, drinking, and beginning any lawful action. The full phrase is Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Raheem (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful).
Praise be to Allah. Said after eating, when grateful, and in prayer. Expresses thanks and acknowledgment that all good comes from Allah.
Glory be to Allah. Said to glorify Allah and affirm He is free from any imperfection. Often said in dhikr and when impressed by creation.
What Allah has willed. Said when admiring something good, to acknowledge that it is by Allah's will and to ward off envy or the evil eye.
glossary.definitionAr: تعظيم قدرة الله وحفظ من العين

glossary.definition: If Allah wills. Said when speaking about future plans, acknowledging that outcomes depend on Allah's decree.
The holy book of Islam, the literal word of Allah revealed to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) through the angel Jibril. Recited in prayer and studied for guidance.
glossary.definitionAr: كلام الله المنزل على النبي محمد

glossary.definition: Reports of the sayings, actions, and approvals of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). With the Quran, a primary source of Islamic belief and practice.
The teachings and example of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)—what he said, did, or approved. Following the Sunnah is central to Islamic practice.
The declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' The first of the Five Pillars; entry into Islam.
glossary.definitionAr: لا إله إلا الله محمد رسول الله

glossary.definition: Ablution; ritual washing before prayer. Involves washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, and feet in a prescribed manner.
The White Days—the 13th, 14th, and 15th of each Islamic month (full moon period). Voluntary fasting on these three days is a recommended Sunnah.
glossary.definitionAr: الثالث عشر والرابع عشر والخامس عشر من الشهر

glossary.definition: Excellence; doing things in the best way. In worship, it is to worship Allah as though you see Him; if you do not see Him, He sees you.
God-consciousness; piety; being mindful of Allah in all that one does. Fasting is prescribed to help develop taqwa (Quran 2:183).
Ongoing charity whose reward continues after one's death. Examples: building a well, teaching beneficial knowledge, planting trees, supporting orphans.
